topic: Day 2 · Acid–Base II — Alkalosis, Respiratory & Mixed Disorders
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: Acute physician and nephrologist who teaches the 'read any ABG in ninety seconds' course and insists that the second half of acid–base — the alkaloses and the mixed pictures — is where the real diagnoses hide.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 68-year-old man is admitted from a nursing home, drowsy and profoundly weak. For a week he has vomited everything — a gastric outlet obstruction from a chronic ulcer. The gas reads: pH 7.58, pCO₂ 6.8 kPa (51 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 46 mmol/L, Na⁺ 138, K⁺ 2.6, Cl⁻ 78. The night SHO frowns: "the CO₂ is high — is he in respiratory failure? Should I worry about his lungs?" No. His lungs are doing exactly what they should. This is a severe metabolic alkalosis from weeks of losing hydrochloric acid down a vomiting bowl, and the high CO₂ is the correct compensation. In session 13 we mastered the acidoses; today we finish the acid–base map — the alkaloses, the respiratory disorders, and the mixed pictures where two or three processes hide inside one gas.

1 · 🧭 Where we left off — and where alkalosis fits

Session 13 gave you the five-step method: pH → primary disorder → expected compensation → anion gap → delta-delta. That method does not change today; we simply turn it on the other two primary disorders (metabolic alkalosis, respiratory acid–base) and then on gases where several processes coexist. The four primary disorders, recapped in one table so the compensation numbers you need are all in one place:

Primary disorderpHPrimary changeExpected compensation
Metabolic acidosis↓↓ HCO₃⁻Winter's: pCO₂ = 1.5×HCO₃⁻ + 8 (±2)
Metabolic alkalosis↑↑ HCO₃⁻pCO₂ rises ~0.7 mmHg per 1 mmol/L HCO₃⁻ rise (≈ +0.7 × ΔHCO₃⁻)
Respiratory acidosis↓↑ pCO₂Acute: HCO₃⁻ +1 per 10 mmHg; Chronic: +4 per 10 mmHg
Respiratory alkalosis↑↓ pCO₂Acute: HCO₃⁻ −2 per 10 mmHg; Chronic: −5 per 10 mmHg
Metabolic alkalosis is the only disorder the body compensates for by hypoventilating — and it is the disorder where compensation is most limited, because you cannot hold your breath forever.
💡 The ceiling on respiratory compensation

To compensate for a metabolic alkalosis the patient must retain CO₂ by breathing less, but hypoxic drive stops this before it gets far — the pCO₂ rarely climbs above ~55 mmHg (7.3 kPa) from compensation alone. So a pCO₂ well above that in an alkalotic patient means a coexisting primary respiratory acidosis, not zealous compensation.

2 · ⚗️ Metabolic alkalosis — the two-hit model (generation + maintenance)

Here is the concept that makes metabolic alkalosis finally make sense. The kidney is a superb bicarbonate-dumping organ — give a healthy person a bicarbonate load and they excrete it in hours. So a sustained metabolic alkalosis is impossible unless two separate things are true. You need a process that generates the alkalosis and, crucially, a second factor that stops the kidney from excreting the excess bicarbonate — the maintenance factor.

Generation — how the bicarbonate appears

  • Loss of acid — vomiting/NG suction strips HCl from the stomach; every H⁺ lost leaves a HCO₃⁻ behind. Renal H⁺ loss via the kidney (hyperaldosteronism, diuretics) does the same.
  • Gain of alkali — bicarbonate infusion, massive citrate (blood transfusion, regional anticoagulation), milk-alkali syndrome.
  • Intracellular shift / contraction — loss of bicarbonate-poor fluid concentrates the bicarbonate that remains (contraction alkalosis, below).

Maintenance — why the kidney won't let go of the bicarbonate

This is the part that is always forgotten and always the key to treatment. Normally the kidney would dump the excess HCO₃⁻. It fails to when:

  • Chloride depletion — the distal nephron needs Cl⁻ to secrete HCO₃⁻ (via pendrin). Vomiting and diuretics deplete chloride, so the kidney physically cannot excrete bicarbonate until you give chloride back. This is why saline cures it.
  • Volume depletion — a contracted circulation drives avid proximal Na⁺ (and hence HCO₃⁻) reabsorption and switches on the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone axis.
  • Potassium depletion — hypokalaemia drives H⁺ into cells and stimulates renal ammoniagenesis and H⁺ secretion, sustaining the alkalosis.
  • Mineralocorticoid excess — aldosterone directly drives distal H⁺ and K⁺ secretion, generating and maintaining alkalosis even when the patient is volume-replete.
Metabolic alkalosis needs a generator AND a maintainer. Treatment targets the maintainer — nearly always chloride, volume and potassium.
🎯 Contraction alkalosis — the "concentration" mechanism

Loop and thiazide diuretics make the patient excrete a large volume of chloride-rich, bicarbonate-poor urine. The extracellular fluid shrinks around a fixed amount of bicarbonate — the bicarbonate is literally concentrated into a smaller volume, raising its measured concentration. Add the chloride and potassium depletion the diuretic also causes, and you have both the generation and the maintenance of a classic saline-responsive alkalosis. It is the commonest metabolic alkalosis on the wards.

3 · 🔬 The pivotal split — urine chloride divides the whole differential

Just as the urine anion gap split the normal-gap acidoses in session 13, a single urine measurement — the urine chloride — splits every metabolic alkalosis into two boxes that are managed completely differently. Note we use urine chloride, not sodium: diuretics and vomiting can spill sodium (as sodium bicarbonate) even when the patient is volume-deplete, so urine sodium misleads. Chloride does not.

Saline-RESPONSIVE (chloride-depleted)Saline-RESISTANT (mineralocorticoid-driven)
Urine Cl⁻< 20 mmol/L (kidney hoarding chloride)> 20 mmol/L (chloride replete)
Volume statusDeplete (or "contracted")Replete or expanded (often hypertensive)
CausesVomiting, NG suction, diuretics (after they stop), post-hypercapnia, villous adenoma, cystic fibrosis sweat lossPrimary hyperaldosteronism (Conn), Cushing, exogenous steroids, liquorice, Liddle, Bartter/Gitelman, severe K⁺ depletion, renal artery stenosis
Blood pressureNormal or lowOften high (except Bartter/Gitelman — normotensive)
TreatmentGive chloride: 0.9% saline + KCl replacementSaline does NOT work — treat the cause: spironolactone/eplerenone, adrenalectomy, stop steroid/liquorice
💡 The one-line rule that runs the workup

Urine chloride < 20 → saline-responsive → give saline. Urine chloride > 20 with hypertension → think mineralocorticoid excess (check aldosterone:renin ratio). Urine chloride > 20 without hypertension → think Bartter/Gitelman or covert diuretic/vomiting abuse.

Why active diuretic use is the exception that proves the rule

While a loop/thiazide diuretic is actively working, it is blocking chloride reabsorption, so the urine chloride is high even though the patient is chloride-deplete and will respond to saline once the drug wears off. Timing matters: measure the urine chloride when the diuretic effect has passed, or you will mislabel a saline-responsive patient as resistant. Surreptitious diuretic abuse (and covert vomiting, where urine Cl⁻ swings with the timing of purging) is the classic diagnostic trap — think of it in the young woman with an unexplained alkalosis and normal blood pressure.

🎯 Bartter vs Gitelman — the "diuretic in the genes"

Bartter syndrome behaves like a permanent loop diuretic (defect in the thick ascending limb, presents in childhood, normal/low calcium excretion issues, can have high urinary calcium). Gitelman behaves like a permanent thiazide (distal tubule, milder, presents in adults, classically hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria). Both give a saline-resistant, normotensive, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — the giveaway is high urine chloride with a normal blood pressure and no diuretics on the chart.

4 · 🩺 Treating metabolic alkalosis — and the potassium you must not forget

The saline-responsive patient is fixed by restoring what was lost: 0.9% sodium chloride to replace volume and chloride, with generous KCl to replace potassium. You cannot correct the alkalosis without correcting the potassium — the two are locked together, because hypokalaemia is itself a maintenance factor. In our opening case (K⁺ 2.6) the potassium deficit is enormous and must be replaced aggressively with cardiac monitoring.

  • Ongoing gastric loss (NG suction, unavoidable vomiting): add a proton-pump inhibitor to cut the acid being lost at source — an elegant, mechanism-based intervention.
  • Diuretic-driven and you cannot stop the diuretic (heart failure): add a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide 250–500 mg) to make the kidney waste bicarbonate — but watch for the hypokalaemia it worsens.
  • Severe (pH > 7.55) with renal failure that cannot excrete bicarbonate: haemodialysis against a low-bicarbonate bath, or (rarely) dilute hydrochloric acid via a central line, is the last resort.
  • Saline-resistant: saline is useless or harmful (many are hypertensive/volume-expanded) — block the mineralocorticoid (spironolactone/eplerenone/amiloride), remove the source (adrenal adenoma, liquorice, exogenous steroid), and replace magnesium and potassium.
⚠️ Severe alkalosis is not benign

A pH above 7.55 is dangerous: it causes cerebral and coronary vasoconstriction, seizures, tetany, arrhythmias, shifts the oxygen-dissociation curve left (impairing tissue O₂ delivery), and — because alkalosis drives potassium and ionised calcium down — precipitates the very arrhythmias that kill. Metabolic alkalosis has a mortality that climbs steeply above pH 7.55. Treat it as the emergency it is, not the afterthought it's often mistaken for.

5 · 🌬️ Respiratory disorders — the acute vs chronic distinction is everything

Respiratory acid–base is driven by one number, the pCO₂, set by alveolar ventilation. The clinical art is telling acute from chronic, because the kidney's metabolic compensation takes 2–5 days to develop. The compensation numbers are the diagnosis of chronicity:

Respiratory acidosis (pCO₂ ↑ — hypoventilation)

HCO₃⁻ rise per 10 mmHg ↑ pCO₂pH change per 10 mmHg
Acute+1 mmol/LpH falls ~0.08
Chronic (renal compensation established)+4 mmol/LpH falls ~0.03

Causes: anything that drops minute ventilation — opioids/sedatives, COPD, neuromuscular disease (Guillain–Barré, myasthenic crisis), chest-wall problems, exhaustion in any severe illness. Reading it: a COPD patient with pCO₂ 70 and HCO₃⁻ 34 has had time to retain bicarbonate (roughly +4 per 10 above 40 → +12 → ~36) — this is chronic and compensated; the same pCO₂ with a HCO₃⁻ of 27 is acute decompensation (only +3) and a ventilatory emergency.

Respiratory alkalosis (pCO₂ ↓ — hyperventilation)

HCO₃⁻ fall per 10 mmHg ↓ pCO₂pH change per 10 mmHg
Acute−2 mmol/LpH rises ~0.08
Chronic−5 mmol/LpH rises ~0.03

Causes — the mnemonic CHAMPS: CNS (stroke, tumour, anxiety/pain), Hypoxia (PE, pneumonia, altitude), Aspirin/salicylate (a direct medullary stimulant — see session 16), Mechanical ventilation (over-ventilated), Progesterone/Pregnancy, Sepsis/liver failure. Respiratory alkalosis is the commonest acid–base disorder in hospital and often the earliest sign of serious illness — the tachypnoeic patient blowing off CO₂ is telling you something is wrong before anything else does.

💡 Chronic respiratory alkalosis is the one disorder that can normalise the pH

Given days, renal compensation for a chronic respiratory alkalosis (e.g. high-altitude, pregnancy, chronic liver disease) can bring the pH almost all the way back to 7.40 — it is the disorder most capable of near-complete compensation. A near-normal pH with a low pCO₂ and low HCO₃⁻ is a fully compensated chronic respiratory alkalosis, not a laboratory error.

6 · 🧩 Mixed disorders — using the numbers to unmask the hidden process

A mixed disorder is two or more primary processes at once. The whole point of calculating expected compensation and the delta-delta (session 13) is that they are the only tools that expose the process the pH is hiding. Three rules find almost every mixed picture:

  1. Compensation that is wrong in magnitude = a second disorder. Too little compensation, or too much, is not the body being lazy or over-eager — the body compensates predictably. Deviation from the expected number is a second primary process. (Winter's for metabolic acidosis; the tables above for the rest.)
  2. Compensation pointing the "wrong way" is impossible. The body never overcompensates into the opposite abnormality. If a metabolic acidosis is accompanied by a frank alkalaemic pH, there is a primary alkalosis on top.
  3. Delta-delta ≠ 1 in a high-gap acidosis = a second metabolic process. Δ ratio < 1 adds a normal-gap acidosis; Δ ratio > 2 adds a metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis (the propped-up bicarbonate).
🎯 The signature mixed pictures to recognise on sight

Salicylate poisoning: a primary respiratory alkalosis (direct medullary stimulation) PLUS a primary high-gap metabolic acidosis — an adult with a near-normal or high pH, low pCO₂ AND low HCO₃⁻ and a high anion gap. Cardiac arrest: metabolic (lactic) acidosis + respiratory acidosis (no ventilation) — the lethal combined acidosis. Severe COPD exacerbation on a loop diuretic: chronic respiratory acidosis + metabolic alkalosis — a startlingly high bicarbonate. The vomiting DKA patient: high-gap acidosis + metabolic alkalosis (delta ratio > 2).

Triple disorders — when three processes coexist

A triple disorder is a high-gap metabolic acidosis + a metabolic alkalosis + a respiratory disorder. You cannot have two primary respiratory disorders at once (the pCO₂ is a single number that is either high or low), so the maximum is: one respiratory + a metabolic acidosis + a metabolic alkalosis. The classic is the alcoholic with vomiting, pancreatitis and aspiration:

  • High-gap metabolic acidosis — alcoholic ketoacidosis / lactate (raised anion gap is the durable fact).
  • Metabolic alkalosis — from the vomiting (unmasked by a delta ratio > 2, propping up the bicarbonate).
  • Respiratory disorder — alkalosis (sepsis/pain) or acidosis (aspiration, obtundation), read off Winter's.
The anion gap finds the acidosis, the delta-delta finds the alkalosis, and Winter's formula finds the respiratory disorder. Three tools, three hidden processes.

7 · 🧑‍⚕️ Worked examples — combining metabolic and respiratory

Example A — the opening case (pure severe metabolic alkalosis)

pH 7.58, pCO₂ 51 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 46, Na 138, K 2.6, Cl 78, urine Cl 8.

  1. pH 7.58 → alkalaemia.
  2. HCO₃⁻ 46 (high) with high pH → metabolic alkalosis is primary.
  3. Expected compensation: pCO₂ should rise ~0.7 × (46−24) = +15 above 40 → ~55 mmHg. Measured 51 → appropriate hypoventilation, no respiratory disorder. (The high CO₂ is compensation, not lung failure.)
  4. Urine Cl 8 (<20) → saline-responsive, fits the vomiting/gastric-outlet history.

Diagnosis & treatment: severe saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis from HCl loss. Give 0.9% saline with aggressive KCl (the K of 2.6 is life-threatening), add a PPI to cut ongoing gastric acid loss, treat the obstruction. Do not ventilate him for the "high CO₂."

Example B — the mixed COPD picture

A COPD patient on furosemide: pH 7.42, pCO₂ 65 mmHg (8.7 kPa), HCO₃⁻ 41, Na 140, Cl 88, K 3.1.

  1. pH 7.42 → almost normal — the trap. Finish every step.
  2. pCO₂ 65 (high) would give acidaemia; HCO₃⁻ 41 (high) would give alkalaemia — two primary disorders cancelling.
  3. Chronic respiratory acidosis alone: expected HCO₃⁻ = 24 + 4×(65−40)/10 = 24 + 10 = 34. Measured is 41 — 7 higher than compensation allows → a coexisting metabolic alkalosis (the loop diuretic).
  4. Low K⁺ 3.1 and low Cl⁻ 88 fit the diuretic-driven, chloride-depleted alkalosis.

Diagnosis: chronic respiratory acidosis + metabolic alkalosis. The normal pH is deceptive; the sky-high bicarbonate is the clue. Correcting the alkalosis (KCl, careful chloride repletion, acetazolamide if the diuretic must continue) actually improves respiratory drive, because the metabolic alkalosis was blunting his ventilation.

Example C — the salicylate mix

pH 7.44, pCO₂ 22 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 15, Na 140, Cl 100, anion gap 25 — a confused adult found with an empty aspirin bottle.

  1. pH 7.44 → near-normal, faintly alkalaemic.
  2. Low pCO₂ (alkalosis) AND low HCO₃⁻ with a high anion gap 25 (acidosis) — two opposing primary processes.
  3. Is the low pCO₂ just compensation for the metabolic acidosis? Winter's: expected pCO₂ = 1.5×15 + 8 = 30.5. Measured is 22 — far lower than compensation → an independent primary respiratory alkalosis.

Diagnosis: the textbook salicylate picture — primary respiratory alkalosis + primary high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The near-normal pH hides two dangerous processes; the raised anion gap and the "too low" pCO₂ give it away. (Management — urinary alkalinisation and dialysis thresholds — is session 16.)

☠️ M&M — the "high CO₂" that got a chest drain and a ventilator

A 74-year-old woman with a bowel obstruction had vomited for ten days. Her gas: pH 7.61, pCO₂ 58 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 52, K⁺ 2.4. The covering team saw the raised CO₂, called it "type 2 respiratory failure," started BiPAP and then intubated her when she grew drowsy — attributing the drowsiness to CO₂ narcosis. On the ventilator they set a high minute volume to "blow off the CO₂." Her pCO₂ fell to 40, the compensation for her metabolic alkalosis was stripped away, her pH shot to 7.72, and she had a run of ventricular tachycardia and a cardiac arrest. What was missed: the raised CO₂ was appropriate respiratory compensation for a severe saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis; the drowsiness was from the alkalosis, profound hypokalaemia (K 2.4) and hypochloraemia — not CO₂ narcosis. Lessons: in an alkalaemic patient a high CO₂ is compensation, never the primary problem; do the five steps before you touch the ventilator; ventilating away compensatory hypercapnia can be lethal. She needed saline, chloride and potassium, not a tube.

8 · 🔁 Contrast card — saline-responsive vs saline-resistant alkalosis

FeatureSaline-RESPONSIVESaline-RESISTANT
Core mechanismChloride + volume depletion the kidney can't overcomeMineralocorticoid excess drives H⁺/K⁺ loss even when replete
Urine chloride< 20 mmol/L> 20 mmol/L
Volume / BPDeplete, normo/hypotensiveReplete/expanded, often hypertensive (Bartter/Gitelman are the normotensive exceptions)
Typical causesVomiting, NG suction, diuretics (worn off), post-hypercapnia, CFConn, Cushing, exogenous steroid, liquorice, Liddle, Bartter/Gitelman, severe K⁺ depletion
Treatment0.9% saline + KCl (± PPI, ± acetazolamide)Aldosterone blockade / treat source; saline is ineffective or harmful
PotassiumLow — replace it, it maintains the alkalosisLow — replace it and remove the driver

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Metabolic alkalosis is a two-hit disease: a generator (acid loss / alkali gain) AND a maintainer (chloride, volume, potassium depletion, or mineralocorticoid excess). Treatment targets the maintainer.
  2. Urine chloride splits the whole differential: <20 = saline-responsive (give saline + KCl); >20 = saline-resistant (block the mineralocorticoid / treat the source). Use chloride, not sodium.
  3. Contraction alkalosis from diuretics is the commonest ward alkalosis — bicarbonate concentrated into a shrunken, chloride-depleted extracellular space.
  4. Respiratory disorders: acute vs chronic is read off the bicarbonate — acidosis +1 (acute) vs +4 (chronic) per 10 mmHg; alkalosis −2 vs −5. The compensation number IS the chronicity diagnosis.
  5. Mixed disorders are found by the numbers, not the pH: wrong-magnitude compensation, impossible over-compensation, or a delta-delta ≠ 1. A normal pH with wild HCO₃⁻ and pCO₂ is two disorders, not health.
  6. Never strip away compensatory hypercapnia in a metabolic alkalosis, and never call a compensating high-CO₂ patient "respiratory failure" without doing the five steps.
  7. Severe alkalosis (pH > 7.55) is a genuine emergency — arrhythmias, seizures, tetany, impaired O₂ delivery — treated by restoring chloride and potassium.

moderatorQs.q: A vomiting patient has a metabolic alkalosis but a urine sodium of 60 mmol/L. Does that make it saline-resistant?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — you asked the wrong ion. In active vomiting, the filtered bicarbonate load spills sodium into the urine as sodium bicarbonate, so urine sodium can be high even though the patient is volume- and chloride-deplete. The discriminating measurement is the urine chloride, which is not fooled by the bicarbonaturia. A urine chloride <20 mmol/L confirms a chloride-depleted, saline-responsive alkalosis — treat with 0.9% saline and generous KCl. Reserve 'saline-resistant' for a high urine chloride, which points to mineralocorticoid excess (usually with hypertension) or a Bartter/Gitelman-type tubulopathy.

moderatorQs.q: A COPD patient has pH 7.34, pCO₂ 70 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 27. Is this acute or chronic, and what does it tell you?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Calculate the expected metabolic compensation. For a chronic respiratory acidosis the bicarbonate should rise ~4 per 10 mmHg of pCO₂ above 40: (70−40)/10 × 4 = +12, giving an expected HCO₃⁻ of ~36. This patient's HCO₃⁻ is only 27 — barely above the acute value (+3 → ~27). So the kidney has not had days to compensate: this is an acute (or acute-on-chronic) respiratory acidosis, i.e. acute ventilatory decompensation. That reframes it as an emergency — the patient is tiring or newly obstructed and needs escalation (bronchodilators, NIV, treat the trigger), not reassurance that 'COPD patients run a high CO₂'.

moderatorQs.q: How can a patient with a completely normal pH still have two serious acid–base disorders?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because compensation and opposing primary disorders can drive the pH in opposite directions until they cancel out. A near-7.40 pH tells you the net effect is neutral, not that nothing is happening. The way you unmask it is to finish the five steps regardless: if the HCO₃⁻ and pCO₂ are both wildly abnormal but the pH is normal, two primary processes are cancelling (e.g. chronic respiratory acidosis + metabolic alkalosis, or salicylate's respiratory alkalosis + high-gap acidosis). The anion gap and the delta-delta then find the metabolic components, and comparing measured pCO₂ against the expected compensation finds the respiratory one. Never stop at a normal pH.

audienceQs.q: My post-op patient on NG suction has a stubborn metabolic alkalosis despite litres of saline. What now?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Two things are usually happening. First, ongoing acid loss — every hour of NG suction strips more HCl, regenerating the alkalosis; start an IV proton-pump inhibitor to cut gastric acid secretion at source. Second, check you have replaced potassium and chloride adequately — hypokalaemia is a maintenance factor and the alkalosis will not lift until K⁺ is restored, so give KCl (as chloride, not other salts) with cardiac monitoring. If the patient is volume-overloaded and you can't give more saline, add acetazolamide 250–500 mg to make the kidney excrete bicarbonate. Reserve dialysis or dilute HCl for a refractory pH >7.55 with renal failure.

audienceQs.q: Why do you keep saying to check urine chloride and not urine sodium in alkalosis, when we use urine sodium everywhere else?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because in metabolic alkalosis the urine sodium lies. When bicarbonate is spilling into the urine (active vomiting, recent diuretic), sodium follows it out as sodium bicarbonate, so a volume-deplete, chloride-starved patient can paradoxically have a high urine sodium. The chloride is the honest marker of the kidney's volume/chloride status: it stays low (<20) exactly when the patient is chloride-deplete and will respond to saline. So for alkalosis specifically, urine chloride is the tool. (Urine sodium remains your friend for AKI and hyponatraemia — different question.)

audienceQs.q: Which drugs on a chart should make me think 'this could be causing a metabolic alkalosis'?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Top of the list: loop and thiazide diuretics — the commonest cause, via chloride/volume/potassium depletion (contraction alkalosis). Then corticosteroids and fludrocortisone and hidden mineralocorticoids like liquorice/carbenoxolone (they mimic aldosterone → saline-resistant alkalosis). Large citrate loads — massive blood transfusion or regional citrate anticoagulation in CRRT — are metabolised to bicarbonate. Antacid/calcium-carbonate excess can cause milk-alkali syndrome. And of course anything driving vomiting. I'd flag the diuretic-plus-low-potassium combination and check whether KCl and, where relevant, a PPI or acetazolamide are needed.
